Text | Er Mu

Editing | Er Mu, Fanyu Meng

In the surreal year of 2020, COVID-19 stopped people traveling, and in 2021, as we wait for vaccines to protect us, most of us are still stuck at home. Everyone travels for different reasons. Some go to see spectacular natural scenery, some to experience other cultures and ways of life, and some perhaps just want to fly to a strange city to feed the pigeons. With international flights still far from back to normal, we have decided to take you out for a stroll to some of the world’s strangest-sounding places. Our first stop: the former empire on which the sun never set, now good old Blighty, the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.

1. Hamilton Mausoleum

Our journey begins in the Scottish Lowlands, in the town of Hamilton in South Lanarkshire, home to a well-known landmark: Hamilton Mausoleum, the resting place of members of the family of the Dukes of Hamilton.

Join a tour here and, besides the curious tales of the ducal family, what else makes the place special? The answer: it is one of the most reverberant man-made spaces in the world. Someone tried it out, and the sound of the door closing takes 15 seconds to die away completely! Such an unusual acoustic space naturally draws many musicians to perform and record there. Watch the video below to hear what playing inside sounds like.

Doesn’t it sound a lot like a church? In fact its reverberation time is longer than that of an ordinary church. Do you like the effect?

2. Sound mirrors

Heading south along the North Sea coast, you’ll come across upright, bowl-shaped concrete structures. These “strange” buildings are called sound mirrors, and they were built to detect and identify enemy aircraft flying in over the North Sea. Just as a concave mirror focuses light, these huge concrete dishes focus the sound of enemy aircraft onto a single point, where a microphone was placed. The largest sound mirrors could detect aircraft more than 10 km away, with an angular accuracy of 1.5 degrees. Once radio radar arrived, however, they quickly became obsolete and were abandoned, and now they are places people visit to take photos.

This sound mirror at Kilnsea in Yorkshire stands 4.5 m tall. During the First World War it was used to give early warning of Zeppelin airships, buying three to four minutes. Between 1915 and 1917, Zeppelins reached northeast England more than 15 times.

In Kent, in the south of England, three sound mirrors stand together. They were built in the 1920s and 1930s, mainly to find out which shape worked best for detection: a 6 m concave dish, a 9 m hemispherical bowl and a 60 m long curved wall.

3. Singing Ringing Tree

Heading west, we come to Burnley, a town north of Manchester. On the nearby Pennine hills stands a strangely shaped tree that “sings” as it looks down over the town. This odd tree is in fact a contemporary art installation, designed and built in 2006 by the noted architects Anna Liu and Mike Tonkin, and it won a Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) award. The 3 m tall sculpture is made of many steel pipes of different lengths stacked together. Some of the pipes are purely structural or decorative; the rest have holes cut into their undersides so that they can sound, and pipes of different lengths sound different pitches. When the prevailing westerly wind blows through, the pipes play together an “unforgettable” song.

Have a listen in the video below:

Does it remind you of anything? A Song of Ice and Fire? Winterfell?

4. High Tide Organ

Further west still, in Blackpool on the west coast, another art installation stands on the seafront promenade. Unlike the Singing Ringing Tree, which is played by the wind, this one is played by the sea! It is usually known as a sea organ. We explained how sea organs make their sound in an earlier post, Croatia’s Sea Organ: it takes more than waves.

5. Squeaking sands

The world has plenty of beaches, but some are a little out of the ordinary: walk on them and the sand squeaks. Porthor beach in Wales is one of them. Nobody has yet worked out exactly why sand squeaks. One theory is that the sound comes from grains rubbing and pressing against each other, but only smooth, rounded grains without sharp edges seem to squeak, which is why not every beach does. Smooth grains are not enough on their own, either: the sand must also have been freshly washed by water, which is why sand in inland deserts rarely squeaks. And here’s the really fussy part: after being washed, it must then dry out in the sun before it will squeak. So be sure to check the weather before you set off!

Roaring deserts: the underground demons of Marco Polo’s tale at work?

6. The Whispering Gallery at St Paul’s Cathedral

Our last stop is Greater London. St Paul’s Cathedral, one of London’s landmarks, stands in the heart of the city, and its striking central dome is home to the famous Whispering Gallery. Climb 256 steps and you reach the circular gallery running around the inside of the dome. Stand at one side, face the wall, and you can hold a whispered conversation with someone 30 m away on the opposite side. That seems to defy common sense. Can it really work so magically? Read our article The romance of the whispering gallery: not a New York travelogue, but a lesson in acoustics, and if you get the chance, go and try it for yourself.

Reference: http://www.sonicwonders.org
